newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Sceptics doubt Taiwan consensus-building forum.
newsitem.headline: Sceptics doubt Taiwan consensus-building forum.

text.p: Can anything be accomplished when the island's brightest and most powerful figures sit down on Monday to iron out their sharp differences and sketch out a grand blueprint for Taiwan's future?
Don't expect too much, analysts say.

Describing the National Development Conference as "a booster shot for democracy", a hopeful sponsoring government said it believed some common ground could be discovered during the ambitious December 23-28 meeting.

"We hope to invite representatives from all fields to discuss national affairs, build consensus and open a new era for the country," President Lee Teng-hui, who doubles as chairman of the ruling Nationalist Party, has said.
A pessimistic newspaper commentary differed sharply.
"We Chinese people love meetings, but what these meetings can actually achieve is another matter," it said.
Analysts and opposition leaders, while acknowledging the need and good intentions of the first all-party meeting since Taiwan's historic March 23 direct presidential election, were sceptical.

"We do not have high expectations, but neither do we think it's completely useless," Chiu Yi-jen, secretary-general of the main opposition Democratic Progressive Party, told Reuters in a telephone interview.

"We all agree there are pressing issues that need to be resolved. There is still a possibility the National Development Conference may actually achieve something," Chiu said. "We are willing to give it a try."

On the agenda for the week-long forum are constitutional reforms and party politics; economic development; and relations between Taiwan and communist China, the island's giant neighbour and sometimes-menacing diplomatic arch-rival.
Participants include senior officials, party and business leaders, investors, academics and other Taiwan elites.

Lu Ya-li, one of 170 selected participants and a prominent political scientist, said eroding electoral support has made the ruling Nationalists feel the urgency of easing confrontation and building consensus in Taiwan's slowly maturing democracy.
"The ruling Nationalist Party's wafer-thin parliamentary majority has made it very difficult to implement policies," said Lu. "It needs to find a way out."

A deeply divided parliament battled over Taiwan's nuclear future for five months after opposition legislators in May cancelled funding for a US$4.1 billion fourth nuclear plant. The ruling party orchestrated its restoration in October.
The state's victory so angered anti-Nationalist forces that they staged brief but fiery riots after the final vote in one of the worst outbreaks of political chaos in a decade.
Analysts warn that such scenes could appear again and again if the ruling and opposition parties refuse to compromise.
Many participants in the National Development Conference said reforms on government systems and the constitution were likely to stir up political storms.
A proposal to abolish or marginalise Taiwan's provincial government already has aroused heated debate, with provincial officials threatening to boycott the conference.

"We can expect results on minor, less-controversial issues, but it will be difficult to iron out fundamental differences," said Lu, who teaches at National Taiwan University. "It's a bit unrealistic to expect to solve long-standing disputes during a meeting that only lasts for a few days."
Democratic Progressive Party leader Chiu said the opposition welcomed consultation but said action was what really mattered.
"It will end up being empty talk if the ruling government is not prepared to implement the agreements," he said.
